The pact, signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, has emerged as an attractive regional security initiative, with other countries, including Syria, considering joining.

Two Turkish officials said Indonesia’s interest was natural, given the close partnership between Ankara and Jakarta, especially in defence industry cooperation.
Indonesia last year signed a deal worth more than $10bn to buy 48 Turkish Kaan fighter jets. It is also acquiring two Istanbul-class frigates under Turkey’s national shipbuilding programme through a $1bn agreement signed in January between Turkish shipbuilder TAIS and Qatar’s Barzan Holding.
Those growing security ties were further underscored earlier this month when Turkey, Indonesia, Pakistan and Qatar signed a memorandum of understanding known as the Badr Pact. The agreement aims to streamline defence industry cooperation and deepen collaboration on the design, production and funding of military systems and platforms.
A spokesperson for the Indonesian embassy told MEE that they could not confirm at this stage whether Indonesia was interested in joining the Mecca Pact.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'I still love you, pal,' Biden told Netanyahu in final phone call
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
'I still love you, pal,' Biden told Netanyahu in final phone call
In his last phone call with Benjamin Netanyahu as US president, Joe Biden told the Israeli prime minister, "I still love you, pal", according to a transcript of the conversation obtained by the Jerusalem Post.
Five days before leaving office, Biden told Netanyahu, "You're a good man", and "I admire you."
“You’ve been through hell. I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through,” Biden said, according to the transcript. “I know we’ve disagreed on occasion but, you know… I still love you, pal.”
The then-US president continued: “I don’t know how you’ve done it all… Next time I think I have a tough job, I’ll think of you… you’re a good man… I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.”
The call took place on 15 January 2025, the day a ceasefire and hostage-release agreement between Israel and Hamas was announced.
The transript appears to clash with Biden's own account of his relationship with Netanyahu in his memoir Promise Me, America , which has just been published.
In excerpts reported by Newsweek, the former president accused Netanyahu of having “Trump-like tendencies” and “bending democratic institutions to serve his personal needs.” Biden also described a lack of trust between them and criticised Netanyahu’s attempt to overhaul Israel’s judiciary.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Amnesty calls for RSF drone strikes on el-Obeid to be investigated as war crimes
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Amnesty calls for RSF drone strikes on el-Obeid to be investigated as war crimes
Amnesty International called on Wednesday for Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone strikes on el-Obeid in Sudan's North Kordofan state to be investigated as war crimes.
The strikes have hit residential areas and civil infrastructure across the city and its surroundings, killing dozens and disrupting public services.
Amnesty investigated nine RSF drone strikes in el-Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026.
Three of the strikes hit residential areas and four struck key civilian infrastructure, including el-Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market. Two targeted moving vehicles in the strategically vital city, which sits on the main route between the capital Khartoum and Darfur in the west.
In all incidents, interviewees told Amnesty they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

data.title: Middle East Eye: What leverage does the UAE have over permanent UN Security Council members?
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
What leverage does the UAE have over permanent UN Security Council members?
Will any permanent member of the United Nations Security Council veto the Emirati candidate from becoming the next secretary-general?
Lana Nusseibeh has denied the UN’s own findings about the UAE’s role in Sudan’s brutal war but remains a contender to lead the organisation.
On Thursday the Security Council is set to hold its next straw poll on the eight candidates vying to succeed Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, as the secretary-general.
It is an informal, anonymous poll on whether members encourage, discourage or have no opinion about a candidate.
Most of the international controversy over the contest for the world body’s highest administrative role has concerned the candidacy of Nusseibeh, a veteran Emirati diplomat.
That's largely due to the United Arab Emirates' role in Sudan’s war, where it is accused of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) - whose mass killings UN investigators say bear the “hallmarks of genocide”.
There is widespread public evidence, including extensive reporting by Middle East Eye, linking the UAE with the supply of arms and other goods to the RSF - although the Emirati government, including Nusseibeh herself, have repeatedly denied it.
The Security Council’s five permanent members - the US, UK, France, China and Russia - are the only countries that can veto candidates.
But diplomatic sources have told MEE that Nusseibeh now has the backing of all five of the members.
Ahead of the straw poll, MEE takes a look at the deep and extensive economic ties the UAE, a tiny but hugely wealthy state in the Gulf, has managed to develop with each of the five nations.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Tim Hortons app sending user data to Israeli cybertech company, advocacy group confirms
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Tim Hortons app sending user data to Israeli cybertech company, advocacy group confirms
The Tim Hortons app has been sharing sensitive user data with Forter, an Israeli cybertech company founded by alumni of the Israeli military's infamous intelligence Unit 8200, Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) has confirmed.
An investigation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) published last week found that the coffee chain app sends data to third-party companies overseas as soon as the app is launched.
Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science at the University of Calgary who scanned the app's network traffic with his team, said the third party built into the app receives enough information to create a digital fingerprint of each device that can be identified later.
Some of the data includes the device's name and unique identifier, details of the device's camera and sensors, and the names of Wi-Fi routers nearby, which can be used to determine the user's location.
"This was beyond the pale," Reardon told the CBC.
Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst, told the CBC that the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service, but the amount of data collected "seems quite excessive" for simply purchasing a cup of coffee.
In its published investigation, CBC did not identify the third party or its location, saying that "accountability rests with the app developer".

UN committee adopts draft resolutions on Palestinian aid, property rights and Israeli occupation
The United Nations General Assembly's Fourth Committee adopted on Wednesday three draft resolutions concerning support for the mandate and operations of the UN Agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), the rights of Palestinian refugees to their properties, and the reaffirmation of the illegality of Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem and the Syrian Golan.
The move was welcomed by Palestine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates, according to Wafa news agency, which called on the international community to honour its obligations to international law and UN resolutions to protect the rights of the Palestinian people.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US sanctions Lebanese nationals, entities over Hezbollah links
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
US sanctions Lebanese nationals, entities over Hezbollah links
The US Treasury Department has imposed sanctions on three Lebanese individuals and three entities, which it accuses of aiding Hezbollah, in its latest effort to destroy the group’s financial networks around the world.
In a statement, the department said it placed them on the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List, without specifying the charges or the evidence against them.
One of the organisations, "Wa Ta’awanu Association", was described as "a charity that provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services".
"The US government will continue to disrupt Iran’s attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added in a post on X.
The Iranian regime’s attempts to infringe on Lebanon’s sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated. The U.S. government will continue to disrupt Iran’s attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies.
— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) November 18, 2026

data.title: Middle East Eye: US re-issues security warnings to citizens in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
US re-issues security warnings to citizens in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia
The US State Department re-issued its security alerts to American citizens in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain on Wednesday.
The warnings were last sent late in October, and call for "heightened vigilance" in both Gulf countries following attacks from Iran and Yemen's Houthis over the last few days.
